textClass.keywords: Antibiotic resistance Mcr-1 gene Escherichia coli Environment

div.p: First report of mcr-1 gene in E. coli from environmental samples in Ecuador • The isolates were obtained from irrigation channels used for agricultural purposes. • The lack of sewage treatment coverage could favor the spread of resistant bacteria. • cgMLST showed a great diversity among the evaluated isolates.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Antibiotic resistance has become a serious and growing global public health threat (Ferri et al., 2017;Hernando-Amado et al., 2019). Its study has traditionally been focused on clinically relevant pathogens; however, the containment of the emergence and spread of antibiotic resistance determinants requires a holistic integration of human, animal and environmental health (Lin et al., 2018;Martinez, 2009). In fact, there is growing evidence of the role of the environment in both the selection and spread of antibiotic-resistant bacteria (ARB) and antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs), especially in anthropogenically-impacted ecosystems (Drieux et al., 2008;Colomer-Lluch et al., 2014;Marti et al., 2014).

Urban sewage represents one of the main sources of ARB and ARGs (Bouki et al., 2013;Novo et al., 2013;Colomer-Lluch et al., 2014;Barancheshme and Munir, 2018), and their discharges (even treated ones) into water bodies could increase the levels of these emerging pollutants in the environment, whereby disturbing the ecological balance (Berglund, 2015;Maestre-Carballa et al., 2019;Swift et al., 2019). Although several studies have demonstrated that urban discharges promote the persistence and spread of antibiotic resistance, limited information is available from developing countries. Moreover, this impact can be exacerbated in countries, where the coverage of sewage treatment is still scarce (WWAP (United Nations World Water Assessment Programme), 2017).

In the case of Ecuador, there is a lack of adequate sewage treatment facilities (WHO, 2019) and recent studies have demonstrated a high prevalence of ARB in anthropogenically-impacted surface waters in Ecuador, compared with those undisturbed systems (Guerrero-Latorre et al., 2018;Ortega-Paredes et al., 2019a). Considering that colistin is a last resort antibiotic for the treatment of multidrug-resistant Gramnegative bacterial infections (Al-Tawfiq et al., 2017;WHO, 2017), this study aimed to characterize the genetic structure of the mcr-1 gene among E. coli isolates recovered from surface waters and sediments in Ecuador. A core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) was also used to assess the relatedness among these isolates.

div.head: Bacterial isolation
div.p: Sampling points, which covered the coastal and Andean regions in Ecuador, were selected according to the spatial suitability criteria, such as population density, agricultural areas, river network, irrigation channels, proximity to hospitals, logistic feasibility, and upstream and downstream areas from the discharge point. Fifty-nine water (1.0 L) and sediment (100 g, depth 1 cm) samples were collected from January to October 2018 from rivers and irrigation channels in the provinces of Pichincha (n = 6), Cotopaxi (n = 12), Tungurahua (n = 15), Manabí (n = 13), and Guayas (n = 13). All samples were collected in sterile containers, transported to the laboratory at 5 °C ± 2 °C, and processed immediately for microbiological analysis and further assays. Briefly, serial dilutions of water and sediment samples, the latter previously homogenized in PBS at pH 7.4 (1:10 w/v), were filtered through 0.45 μm cellulose membrane filters (Merck Millipore; Darmstadt, Germany) and placed on both Chromocult agar according to the ISO 9308 (International Organization for Standardization, 2014) and MacConkey agar (Merck Millipore) (Sigma-Aldrich; St. Louis, USA). After the incubation period at 37 °C for 24 h, blue-violet colonies in Chromocult agar and both lactosepositive and negative colonies in MacConkey agar were purified and cryopreserved with 15% glycerol. Up to 10 colonies from each sampling site were analyzed to avoid the isolation of clonal bacteria.

div.head: PCR detection of mcr genes and bacterial identification
div.p: All isolates were screened via PCR to detect the presence of genes conferring resistance to colistin such as mcr-1, mcr-2, mcr-3, mcr-4, and mcr-5. Moreover, all isolates positive for mcr genes were further evaluated for the presence of β-lactamase genes such as bla IMI , bla KPC , bla OXA-48 , bla NDM , bla VIM , bla TEM, and bla CTX-M groups. PCR amplification was performed in a total volume of 12.5 μL using DreamTaq Green PCR Mastermix 6.3 μL (Thermo Fisher Scientific; Waltham, MA, USA), 0.3 μL of each primer (10 μM stock), 4.3 μL of nuclease-free water (Thermo Fisher Scientific), and 1.3 μL of total DNA. All primers used in this study are described in Supplementary Table S1. Amplification was carried out as follows: initial denaturation at 95 °C for 1 min; 35 cycles of 95 °C for 30 s, annealing (temperatures given in Supplementary Table S1) for 30 s, extension at 72 °C for 1 min; and a final elongation step at 72 °C for 7 min. An aliquot of 10 μL of each PCR product was analyzed via agarose gel electrophoresis and stained using SYBR® Safe DNA Gel Stain (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, USA). Positive amplicons were then sequenced by Elim Biopharm (Hayward, USA). Moreover, mcrpositive isolates were identified using the MALDI Biotyper system (Bruker Daltonik GmbH, Bremen, Germany).

div.head: Whole genome sequencing
div.p: The whole genome of all isolates positive for mcr genes was sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego, CA, USA). In order to determine the genetic environment of mcr genes, the sequences were assembled into contigs using QIAGEN CLC Genomics Workbench version 10.0 (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) (Bankevich et al., 2012), whose assemblies were screened to identify the contig carrying the mcr gene using the BLASTN application (Camacho et al., 2009) with the resistance gene sequence as the query sequence. The identified contigs were then aligned against a previously curated database of complete Enterobacteriaceae plasmids (Orlek et al., 2017), as well as against reference genomes using the GenBank database (https://www.ncbi. nlm.nih.gov/genbank/). The results were visualized using the Easyfig program (Sullivan et al., 2011).

div.head: Molecular typing of mcr-positive isolates
div.p: Seven loci (adk, fumC, gyrB, icd, mdh, purA and recA), previously described for E. coli, were used for the initial MLST analysis. A core genome MLST (cgMLST) scheme for E. coli was created using Ridom SeqSphere+ software v7.0 (Jünemann et al., 2013), with the E. coli K-12 genome as reference. The cgMLST scheme containing 3166 gene targets was used to investigate the relatedness among the isolates and with those mcrpositive isolates previously reported in other countries (Supplementary Table S2). Six mcr-negative E. coli isolates were also included in the analysis, which were previously isolated from clinical samples in Ecuador. Genome assemblies were also uploaded to the Center for Genomic Epidemiology to extract information on ARGs and plasmid replicons for E. coli using ResFinder 4.1 and PlasmidFinder 2.1, respectively (Bortolaia et al., 2020;Carattoli et al., 2014).

div.head: Conjugation assays and antibiotic susceptibility testing
div.p: Conjugation assays were performed using E. coli J53 as the recipient strain, as previously described (Liu et al., 2015). The donor-recipient ratio was 1:1 using nutrient agar supplemented with colistin sulfate (0.5 μg/mL) and sodium azide (100 μg/mL) as the selective medium. The transconjugants were analyzed via the Vitek® 2 Compact system (BioMérieux; Marcy-lEtoile, France) to compare their susceptibility profiles with the donor strain. The Sensititre System with ARGNF plates was used to determine the antimicrobial susceptibility of E. coli transconjugants. Minimum inhibitory concentrations of piperacillin/tazobactam (TPZ), ceftazidime (CAZ), cefotaxime (CTX), cefepime (FEP), aztreonam (ATM), ertapenem (ETP), imipenem (IPM), meropenem (MEM), amikacin (AMK), gentamicin (GEN), ciprofloxacin (CIP), Trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (SXT) and colistin (COL) were evaluated according to the CLSI guidelines (Clinical and Laboratory Standars Institute, 2020). Phenotypic β-lactamase production (ESBL) was evaluated via a double-disk synergy test (Drieux et al., 2008). Phenotypic testing for carbapenemase type KPC was performed via the boronic acid combined-disk test (PBA) (Tsakris et al., 2009). An EDTA-disk synergy test was used to identify metallo-β-lactamase-producing strains among the mcr-1 positive isolates and their transconjugants, as previously described (Yan et al., 2004).

div.head: Results and discussion
div.p: A total of 459 Enterobacteriaceae-like-morphology isolates were recovered from different sites and dates. Among them, only 4 isolates carried mcr genes as demonstrated by PCR amplification. Moreover, MALDI-TOF analysis revealed that mcr-positive isolates are Escherichia coli. The details about the origin and source of the isolates are shown in Supplementary Table S3.

Multidrug-resistant phenotypes were detected, showing an extended-spectrum β-lactamases (ESBL) phenotype in all mcr-positive E. coli isolates (Supplementary Table S4). All mcr-positive E. coli isolates were classified as non-wild type (NWT) according to their colistin MIC determination (>4 mg/L). Additionally, all the isolates showed ESBL phenotype and resistance to clinically-relevant antibiotics such as cefotaxime, ceftazidime, cefepime and aztreonam (Supplementary Table S4). All mcr-positive E. coli isolates co-harbored different βlactamases that include bla TEM-1B , bla CTX-M-15 (U175), bla CTX-M-55 (U20), and bla CTX-M-65 (U30 and U144). In Ecuador, the first reported clinical E. coli isolates carrying the mcr-1 gene co-harbored the bla CTX-M-55 variant (Ortega-Paredes et al., 2016), whereas E. coli isolates carrying both mcr-1 and bla CTX-M-65 genes were detected in humans, chickens and dogs (Loayza-Villa et al., 2019;Ortega-Paredes et al., 2019b). However, no reports have described E. coli co-harboring mcr-1 and bla CTX-M-15 genes in Ecuador to date. Moreover, conjugation assays were successful in three E. coli isolates (U20, U30 and U144), and their transconjugants carried the mcr-1 gene and β-lactamases, indicating the presence of these genes on a plasmid.

Genome analysis revealed that all mcr sequences shared 100% nucleotide identity with the sequence of mcr-1 that was first found in 2015 in China (Liu et al., 2016). Although the genetic environment of mcr-1 was similar in 3 (U20, U30 and U144) of out 4 isolates, phenotypic and genotypic antibiotic resistance features were different among these isolates. Moreover, the genetic environment of mcr-1 in these isolates was different to those described for the first time in China (Fig. 1); however, they were similar to those described in plasmids from E. coli isolated from animal and municipal wastewater samples in Japan (Hayashi et al., 2019) and patients in Australia (Ellem et al., 2017). The genetic environment surrounding mcr-1 showed that the nikB gene was present in the upstream region (although ISApI1 was found to be absent), whereas the pap2 and ydfA genes were present in the downstream region.

Interestingly, the mcr-1 gene was chromosomally located in one isolate (U175), and the genetic environment, in which two copies of ISApI1 is flanking mcr-1, was similar to those exclusively described in some E. coli chromosomes from Japan and Vietnam (GenBank accession numbers: LC424789, LC424782 and AP021890). These results support our previous observations because transconjugation assays failed in E. coli U175.

The cgMLST analysis showed that the E. coli isolates belong to different lineages (Fig. 2), which include the ST10 (isolate U175) that has been detected in mcr-positive E. coli of animal origin from Spain (Migura-Garcia et al., 2020) and clinical samples from Colombia (Saavedra et al., 2017) and China (Huang et al., 2020). Moreover, the ST5876 (isolate U144), commonly associated with animal origin (Zhou et al., 2020), has been detected in mcr-positive E. coli in Japan, the Netherlands and Spain (Fig. 2). The ST58 (isolate U30) belonging to the ST155 complex has recently been associated with mcr-positive E. coli from a wide variety of sources (animal, human, environmental). However, no reports of E. coli belonging to ST10779 (isolate U20) have been found to harbor mcr genes. Likewise, all the isolates harbored a wide diversity of aminoglycoside, β-lactam, phenicol and tetracycline resistance genes (Table 1), whose occurrence has usually been associated with isolates harboring the mcr-1 gene in samples of human, animal and food origin (Hammad et al., 2019;Kassem et al., 2021;Migura-Garcia et al., 2020). Moreover, in silico plasmid replicon typing revealed that mcr-positive E. coli isolates harbored multiple plasmid replicons (Table 1).

Due to the limited number of mcr-positive E. coli is impossible to find an epidemiological connection between the lack of adequate sewage treatment, and their subsequent discharges into water bodies, and the occurrence of these isolates in water bodies in Ecuador. However, untreated sewage discharges represent a serious risk in terms of food and water safety. The Cutuchi River receives untreated urban sewage from the city of Latacunga and rural parishes, thereby estimating their impact in 30,000 m 3 of sewage/day and 18 tons/day of garbage and waste from domestic origin, unofficial dumps, hospitals, dead animals, and industrial sewage (GAD Latacunga, 2014). Currently, the council of Latacunga is constructing a wastewater treatment plant that will provide wastewater treatment for 170,000 inhabitants, according to the last population census (GAD Latacunga, 2021;INEC, 2010). However, considering the lack of adequate sanitary facilities in other points of the basin, the potential effect of this construction and future operation would not be enough to reduce the presence of these biological contaminants.

In addition, the Latacunga-Salcedo-Ambato irrigation channel receives its main supply from the Cutuchi River, which is impacted by untreated urban sewage discharges from Latacunga city and their surrounding rural areas. It should be noted that this water supply is used for agricultural purposes and there is no evidence about its influence on the sanitary quality of surrounding areas. It is necessary therefore to establish an adequate monitoring system that evaluates deeply their impact on the environment and on the influenced population.

div.head: Conclusions
div.p: In this work, we reported for the first time the presence of multidrug-resistant E. coli harboring the mcr-1 gene from water bodies and their sediments in Ecuador. This suggests the circulation of mcrpositive E. coli isolates in the environment, which could have an anthropogenic origin, including urban wastewater discharges and livestock facilities. These findings pose a potential threat to public health, considering both that the isolates were obtained from irrigation channels used for agricultural purposes and that the isolates showed multidrug-resistant phenotypes. Finally, this study puts in evidence the necessity to take suitable measures that minimize the spread of multidrug-resistant bacteria in water bodies in Ecuador.
Supplementary data to this article can be found online at https://doi. org/10.1016/j.scitotenv.2021.150566.
